subject: Archaeology
title: Fire: When Humans Tamed Flames
description: A quick win: understand Fire: When Humans Tamed Flames.

hook.text: Controlling fire was the most important thing humans ever did. It changed our bodies, our brains, and our diet.

buildup.text: The earliest possible hearths date to one million years ago at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa.

discovery.text: Cooking breaks down tough plant fibers and kills parasites in meat.

twist.text: Richard Wrangham argues that cooking shrank our guts and grew our brains. Fire literally reshaped human anatomy.

climax.text: Fire also created campfires — the first gathering place. Socializing around flames may have driven language evolution.

punchline.text: Fire cooked our food, grew our brains, and started our conversations.

quiz.question: How did cooking with fire affect human evolution according to Richard Wrangham?
options: It allowed humans to survive in colder climates
It shrank our guts and allowed our brains to grow larger
It eliminated the need for stone tools

details.summary: Controlled use of fire emerged at least 400,000 years ago, though some evidence suggests much earlier use. Fire transformed human life by enabling cooking, providing warmth and protection, extending the day, and creating social gathering spaces that may have fostered language development.
details.whyItMatters: Fire was the first force of nature humans controlled. Cooking especially transformed human biology by making food more digestible, freeing energy for brain growth and reducing the need for large guts and powerful jaws.
takeaways: Controlled fire use dates to at least 400,000 years ago
Cooking transformed human biology and enabled brain growth
Fire created social spaces that may have fostered language

faq.question: How do archaeologists detect ancient fire use?
faq.answer: Through burned bones, charcoal, heat-altered sediments, and reddened stones. Microscopic analysis can distinguish natural wildfires from controlled hearths by looking for repeated burning in the same location, which indicates intentional fire maintenance.

faq.question: Did cooking really change human evolution?
faq.answer: Richard Wrangham argues convincingly that cooking was transformative. Cooked food yields more calories with less chewing and digestion effort. This energy surplus may have fueled brain expansion, reduced tooth and jaw size, and shaped our uniquely human digestive system.
